title: THE QUEEN WHO DISAPPEARED, THE WOMAN WHO TOOK HER PLACE—AND THE DISTURBING QUESTION HIDING BETWEEN ESTHER AND SARAH
paragraphs:
THE QUEEN WHO DISAPPEARED, THE WOMAN WHO TOOK HER PLACE—AND THE DISTURBING QUESTION HIDING BETWEEN ESTHER AND SARAH
Does the story of Vashti, Xerxes, and Esther somehow echo Sarah, Abraham, and Hagar? The similarities are haunting. The differences are crucial. And buried beneath both stories is a warning about human power, wounded people, impatient hearts—and the God who can still write redemption through what human beings have broken.
There is an uncomfortable moment in the Bible that most of us read too quickly.
A woman disappears.
Another woman takes her place.
And history keeps moving.
In Genesis, Hagar enters Abraham and Sarah’s fractured household because Sarah cannot bear the waiting any longer.
In Esther, Vashti disappears from the royal story after refusing the king’s command, and eventually another woman—Esther—is crowned in her place.
At first glance, the resemblance feels almost impossible to ignore.
Sarah. Hagar. Abraham.
Vashti. Esther. Ahasuerus—commonly identified with the Persian king Xerxes.
Two powerful households.
Two women whose lives become entangled around one man.
Two stories involving status, displacement, beauty, vulnerability, power, and a dramatic reversal.
Two stories in which one woman eventually occupies a place the other does not.
So perhaps you have wondered:
Is Esther’s story secretly repeating Sarah’s?
Is Vashti somehow another Hagar?
Is Esther another Sarah?
And if so… what is God trying to tell us?
The answer is more beautiful—and more sobering—than forcing the characters into matching boxes.
Because there are echoes.
There are striking echoes.
But they are not identical stories, and the Bible never tells us that Vashti represents Hagar or that Esther represents Sarah.
That distinction matters.
Scripture should be allowed to say what Scripture says—and we should be careful not to make it say what it does not.
Paul himself gives Sarah and Hagar an inspired theological interpretation in Galatians 4:21–31. He uses their story figuratively in discussing two covenants, slavery and freedom, flesh and promise.
The Bible never gives Vashti and Esther that same interpretation.
So we must not preach as doctrine what Scripture presents only as a possible literary resemblance.
But once we understand that boundary, something remarkable appears.
Because when these stories are placed beside one another—not as identical allegories, but as biblical narratives involving broken human choices—we begin seeing something painfully familiar.
We begin seeing ourselves.
Genesis 16 opens with words that carry enormous emotional weight:
“Now Sarai, Abram’s wife, had borne him no children.”
Years of waiting are compressed into one sentence.
Years of watching.
Years of wondering.
Years of carrying a promise while her body seemed to contradict it.
God had promised Abraham descendants.
But the nursery remained empty.
And eventually Sarah did what human beings have been doing ever since Eden:
She tried to help God accomplish what God had promised.
Genesis 16:2 preserves the terrible beauty of that moment in Hebrew:
“הִנֵּה־נָא עֲצָרַנִי יְהוָה מִלֶּדֶת”
“Hinnēh-nā ʿăṣāranî YHWH milledet…”
In essence:
“Look, the LORD has prevented me from bearing children.”
Then comes her solution:
“בֹּא־נָא אֶל־שִׁפְחָתִי”
“Go in to my servant…”
And Abram listened.
That sentence should hurt.
Because sometimes faith does not collapse because people stop believing God exists.
Sometimes faith collapses because people still believe the promise…
but stop trusting God’s timing.
Sarah knew the promise.
Abraham knew the promise.
Yet pain whispered:
Maybe God needs your help.
Maybe waiting means God has forgotten.
Maybe you need to manufacture what heaven has not yet delivered.
And standing inside their attempt to solve the problem was another human being.
Hagar.
Not a theological object.
Not a disposable plot device.
A woman.
An Egyptian servant.
A person with a name.
A person whose body became entangled in somebody else’s desperation.
Sarah gave Hagar to Abraham, Hagar conceived, relationships deteriorated, contempt entered the household, anger followed, and eventually Hagar fled into the wilderness.
Genesis does not sanitize what happened.
Its Hebrew description of Sarah’s treatment of Hagar is severe:
“וַתְּעַנֶּהָ שָׂרַי”
“Vatteʿannēhā Sarai…”
Sarah afflicted or dealt harshly with her.
And Hagar ran.
Think about that.
The household carrying God’s promise became a place someone needed to escape.
That should destroy our comfortable categories.
Because being connected to God’s promise does not mean every decision you make is righteous.
Being chosen does not make cruelty holy.
Being wounded does not give us permission to wound someone else.
Sarah had suffered.
But suffering people can still hurt people.
Abraham was a man of faith.
But men of faith can still fail morally.
And Hagar was a servant living inside a complicated household…
but God saw her.
That may be one of the most beautiful reversals in Genesis.
Human beings used her.
God found her.
Human beings defined her by usefulness.
God addressed her personally.
Human beings pushed her toward the margins.
God met her in the wilderness.
Hagar eventually called the LORD:
“אַתָּה אֵל רֳאִי”
“Attah El Ro’i.”
“You are a God who sees me.”
The woman everyone else could treat like part of their solution discovered that she had never been invisible to God.
Remember that.
We are coming back to it.
Because centuries later another woman is standing inside another palace.
Her name is Vashti.
The king is Ahasuerus, traditionally and commonly associated with Xerxes I.
The book of Esther opens with almost obscene magnificence.
Gold.
Silver.
Marble.
Royal wine.
Military leaders.
Nobles.
Power.
For 180 days the king displays “the riches of his royal glory.”
Then comes another seven-day feast.
And on the seventh day, when the king’s heart is merry with wine, he commands that Queen Vashti be brought before the gathered men wearing her royal crown so that her beauty can be displayed.
Scripture tells us why:
She was beautiful.
And Vashti refuses.
That is where interpreters must be careful.
The Bible does not explicitly tell us why she refused.
It does not tell us everything she was thinking.
It does not authorize us to invent secret motives and preach them as revelation.
It simply tells us:
She refused.
And the king became furious.
Then something revealing happens.
The crisis becomes bigger than one marriage.
The king’s advisers fear that women throughout the empire will hear what Vashti did and begin despising their husbands.
One woman's “no” suddenly becomes a national emergency.
A royal decree follows.
Vashti loses her royal position.
And eventually another young woman enters the story.
Esther.
A Jewish orphan raised by Mordecai.
A young woman living among an exiled people.
A woman carrying an identity the palace initially does not know.
And Esther 2:17 says:
“וַיֶּאֱהַב הַמֶּלֶךְ אֶת־אֶסְתֵּר מִכָּל־הַנָּשִׁים וַתִּשָּׂא־חֵן וָחֶסֶד לְפָנָיו…”
“Vayye’ehav hammelekh et-Estēr… vattissa-ḥēn vāḥesed lefanav…”
The king loved Esther more than the other women, and she obtained favor and kindness before him.
Then:
“וַיָּשֶׂם כֶּתֶר־מַלְכוּת בְּרֹאשָׁהּ”
He placed the royal crown upon her head.
And the Hebrew concludes:
“וַיַּמְלִיכֶהָ תַּחַת וַשְׁתִּי”
He made her queen “instead of Vashti.”
There it is.
The sentence that makes the comparison tempting.
One woman.
Another woman.
One position.
Another occupying it.
Hagar enters Abraham’s household because Sarah cannot produce what she desperately wants.
Esther enters the royal position after Vashti has been removed.
But this is precisely where we must refuse an easy equation.
Vashti is not Hagar.
Esther is not Sarah.
Xerxes is certainly not Abraham.
And their stories move in profoundly different theological directions.
Hagar was Sarah’s servant and was given to Abraham as a secondary wife in an attempt to obtain offspring.
Vashti was already queen.
Esther did not engineer Vashti’s removal.
Sarah actively initiated the Hagar arrangement.
Esther did not.
Hagar bore Abraham a son.
Vashti’s story in Esther concerns royal authority, refusal, removal, and replacement—not the fulfillment of a covenant promise through childbirth.
And perhaps most importantly, Scripture itself later interprets Sarah and Hagar covenantally.
Paul writes in Galatians that these women may be understood figuratively in relation to two covenants. He contrasts slavery with freedom and human flesh with divine promise.
No inspired biblical writer tells us to map that symbolism onto Vashti and Esther.
So what are we allowed to see?
Something subtler.
Something painfully human.
Both stories expose what happens when people become pieces inside somebody else’s struggle for control.
Hagar becomes part of Sarah and Abraham’s attempt to resolve barrenness.
Vashti becomes the center of a royal crisis involving the king’s authority and male anxiety throughout an empire.
Esther enters a Persian royal system she did not create.
And suddenly the Bible begins asking us a question far more personal than:
“Which woman represents which woman?”
The question becomes:
What do you do when somebody else’s choices change your life?
That is where some of you stopped reading comfortably.
Because you know.
You know what it feels like to inherit a situation you did not create.
Someone cheated.
You suffered.
Someone left.
You raised the children.
Someone lied.
You lost the friendship.
Someone abused authority.
You carried the wound.
Someone made a selfish decision twenty years ago…
and you are still fighting the consequences today.
Maybe you were Hagar.
Pulled into someone else’s dysfunction.
Maybe you understand Vashti—the terrifying moment when one decision closes a door permanently.
Maybe you understand Esther.
You did not ask for this position.
You did not design this story.
You simply woke up one day and discovered that life had placed you somewhere you never imagined standing.
And maybe you understand Sarah more than you want to admit.
You waited.
And waited.
And waited.
Until waiting became unbearable.
So you forced something.
Manipulated something.
Entered a relationship you knew was wrong.
Made the deal.
Sent the message.
Returned to the addiction.
Compromised.
Panicked.
Tried to manufacture an answer because heaven seemed silent.
And now you are living inside something you created while trying to escape the pain of waiting.
Be honest.
This hit harder than you expected.
Because the most frightening thing about Sarah’s mistake is not that she did not believe in God.
It is that she knew God…
and still tried to control the outcome.
That is us.
We pray…
then manipulate.
We surrender…
then grab it back.
We say, “Your will be done”…
then spend the next week trying to make sure our will happens.
We want Isaac.
But we are terrified of waiting for Isaac.
So we manufacture Ishmael.
And then we blame God for the complications created by our impatience.
Yet Genesis refuses to end Hagar’s story with human failure.
God finds her.
This is where grace enters the scandal.
Not because sin does not matter.
Not because Abraham and Sarah’s actions were harmless.
Not because broken choices magically become righteous choices.
Grace does something far more astonishing.
Grace walks into consequences human beings created…
and God remains God there.
He sees Hagar.
He hears Ishmael.
He keeps His covenant promise concerning Isaac.
He continues dealing with Abraham.
He does not abandon Sarah.
The failures are real.
The consequences are real.
And somehow the faithfulness of God is still more real.
Then Esther gives us another breathtaking picture.
God’s name is famously absent from the Hebrew text of Esther.
No dramatic verse says, “And God appeared.”
No Red Sea splits.
No fire falls from heaven.
No prophet stands before the throne saying, “Thus says the LORD.”
And yet providence seems to breathe through the entire story.
A queen is removed.
An orphaned Jewish girl becomes queen.
Mordecai uncovers a conspiracy.
A genocidal plot develops.
A sleepless king asks for records to be read.
Timing intersects with timing.
One apparently ordinary event touches another…
until the Jewish people are delivered from destruction.
God seems hidden.
But hidden is not the same as absent.
Somebody reading this desperately needs that sentence.
God seems hidden.
But hidden is not the same as absent.
Maybe you cannot see Him in your marriage right now.
Maybe you cannot see Him in the unanswered prayer.
Maybe you cannot see Him in the hospital corridor.
Maybe you cannot see Him in your finances.
Maybe you cannot see Him in the child who walked away from faith.
Maybe your life feels less like Exodus—with oceans opening dramatically—and more like Esther, where providence moves quietly behind ordinary events.
Do not confuse silence with abandonment.
Do not confuse invisibility with inactivity.
Esther could not see the ending from the beginning.
Neither can you.
And here the comparison with Sarah becomes especially powerful—not because Esther “is” Sarah, but because both narratives confront the human obsession with knowing how the story will end.
Sarah thought barrenness was the end.
It was not.
Hagar thought the wilderness was the end.
It was not.
Vashti disappears from the biblical narrative after her removal, and Scripture does not tell us the rest of her personal story. We should have the humility not to invent it.
Esther could have thought being an orphan in exile defined her future.
It did not.
Mordecai could have thought Haman’s decree was the end.
It was not.
The cross looked like the end.
It was not.
And now we have reached the center of everything.
Because Esther is not ultimately about teaching us how to become queens.
Genesis is not ultimately a self-help manual about getting our dreams.
The Bible is moving toward Someone greater.
Jesus Christ.
Every human ruler eventually exposes the limits of human power.
Xerxes possessed an empire stretching across provinces, yet he could not rule the human heart.
Abraham received extraordinary promises, yet Abraham himself needed grace.
Sarah carried the covenant line, yet Sarah needed grace.
Hagar was wounded and vulnerable, and Hagar needed grace.
Esther became queen, but Esther could not conquer humanity’s deepest enemy.
Neither could Mordecai.
Neither could Isaac.
Neither could Israel.
Neither can you.
Neither can I.
We need a better King.
And Jesus is nothing like the intoxicated king displaying his glory before powerful men.
Christ possesses true glory…
yet Philippians tells us He humbled Himself.
The King became a servant.
The Holy One touched lepers.
The Creator washed feet.
The Judge allowed Himself to be judged by sinful men.
The One worthy of every crown accepted a crown of thorns.
And instead of sacrificing others to preserve His throne…
Jesus sacrificed Himself to save His enemies.
That is the Gospel.
We were not innocent heroes waiting to discover our royal destiny.
We were sinners.
We have manipulated.
We have lusted.
We have lied.
We have envied.
We have used people.
We have tried to control outcomes.
We have hidden secret sins beneath religious language.
We have tried to manufacture what only God can provide.
Yet Christ came for sinners.
At the cross, justice and mercy meet.
Jesus bears sin.
Jesus dies.
Jesus is buried.
Jesus rises.
And forgiveness is offered not to people who successfully rewrite their own stories…
but to people willing to repent and trust the One who can.
Maybe that is why these ancient stories still hurt.
Because underneath the palaces, tents, crowns, servants, kings, queens and empires…
there are human hearts.
Scared hearts.
Jealous hearts.
Wounded hearts.
Controlling hearts.
Lonely hearts.
Ambitious hearts.
Hearts desperate to be seen.
Hearts terrified of being replaced.
Hearts afraid that God has forgotten them.
And Jesus still comes for hearts like these.
Maybe you have spent years identifying yourself by the worst chapter.
Divorced.
Rejected.
Abandoned.
Addicted.
Unfaithful.
Betrayed.
Used.
Forgotten.
Ashamed.
Maybe someone else wrote a sentence into your life you never wanted.
Or maybe the hardest truth is this:
You wrote it yourself.
You made the decision.
You crossed the line.
You knew better.
And every time you remember it, shame whispers:
That is who you are now.
No.
Your sin must be faced honestly.
Repentance is not pretending it never happened.
Grace is not God calling evil good.
The Gospel is infinitely better than denial.
The Gospel says your sin can be confessed, judged at the cross, forgiven through Christ, and no longer possess the authority to write the final sentence of your identity.
“If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation.”
That is why repentance is not humiliation without hope.
Repentance is coming home.
It is laying down the exhausting attempt to control everything.
It is Sarah releasing the need to manufacture the promise.
It is Hagar discovering that God sees the forgotten.
It is Esther walking toward the dangerous place where obedience may cost something.
And ultimately it is the sinner falling before Jesus and saying:
“I cannot save myself.”
Maybe that prayer needs to happen now.
Not tomorrow.
Not after you fix yourself.
Now.

Jesus Christ, I have sinned. I have tried to control what belonged to You. I have wounded people. I have hidden things. I have trusted myself more than Your Word. Forgive me. I believe You died for sinners and rose again. I surrender what I cannot repair. Teach me to follow You. Rewrite what sin has broken in me—not according to my desires, but according to Your will. Make my life belong to You.
Be honest.
Not because sharing a Facebook article earns favor with God. It does not.
Send it to the woman who feels replaced.
Send it to the man carrying regret over choices he cannot undo.
Send it to the believer wondering where God went.

If you want your online life to glorify God, one practical way is to use the reach you already have to put Christ-centered truth in front of people who may never walk into a church. Sharing Scripture-rooted content and financially supporting Gospel work can be meaningful acts of stewardship when they flow from love for Christ—not guilt, coercion, or an attempt to purchase God’s favor.
But the deeper reason to stay is not merchandise.
It is discipleship.
It is staying close to Scripture.
It is being challenged when compromise becomes comfortable.
It is being encouraged when faith becomes exhausting.
It is helping Gospel truth travel farther.
Because someday the waiting may become unbearable again.
Someday you may be tempted to manufacture an answer.
Someday somebody you love may feel discarded.
Someday God may seem completely absent from the chapter you are living.
Come back and remember.
Sarah was waiting.
Hagar was wandering.
Esther was hidden.
Mordecai was threatened.
Israel was endangered.
The cross was sealed behind a stone.
And none of those moments had the final word.
Jesus did.
So no—the Bible does not authorize us to say Vashti is Hagar, Esther is Sarah, or Xerxes is Abraham.
But their stories can stand beside one another and expose something astonishing about the human condition.
We fear being replaced.
We fear being forgotten.
We fear waiting.
We fear losing control.
So human beings manipulate, grasp, wound, run, hide and attempt to write endings before God has finished the sentence.
But Scripture keeps pointing beyond human failure toward the faithfulness of God.
And finally toward Jesus Christ.
The King who sees the discarded.
The Savior who receives the repentant.
The Shepherd who searches for the wandering.
The Redeemer who can take a life fractured by other people’s sins—and by our own—and make something holy from the surrendered pieces.
Let your feed become more than entertainment. Let it become a place where Scripture interrupts despair, conviction interrupts compromise, and the Gospel keeps pointing exhausted people back to Jesus.
But above everything else…
Come to Christ.
Christian merchandise cannot save you.
Abraham cannot save you.
Sarah cannot save you.
Esther cannot save you.
Religion cannot save you.
Your good intentions cannot save you.
Only Jesus Christ saves.
And perhaps the line you need to carry away from these women, these wounds, these palaces, these tents and these ancient scandals is this:
What looked like the chapter that ruined everything may become the very place where you discover that God was never finished writing.
